items.quote: He had people working his fields and vineyards in the hills and in the fertile lands, for he loved the soil.
items.contrast: Uzziah’s love motivates the farm work, not the workers’ love of the soil.
items.reason: The pronouns “his” and “he” continue to refer to Uzziah, and “for” links his love of the soil to having people work his land.

items.quote: their illnesses were cured and the evil spirits left them.
items.contrast: The evil spirits leave the sick people, whereas their illnesses are cured rather than said to leave.
items.reason: The key matches the thing explicitly said to leave. However, “the people” and “the items” are avoidably generic, and “on the items’ arrival” is an awkward rendering of handkerchiefs and aprons being taken to the sick.

items.quote: After talking until daylight, he left.
items.contrast: Paul talks until daylight immediately before leaving; breaking bread and eating happens earlier.
items.reason: The sentence directly establishes the final action before Paul’s departure, requiring the reader to distinguish it from his earlier meal.

items.quote: But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to David’s rescue; he struck the Philistine down and killed him.
items.contrast: Abishai kills the Philistine Ishbi-Benob, not David, whom he rescues.
items.reason: Coming to David’s rescue identifies David as the person protected, while “the Philistine” refers to Ishbi-Benob as the one Abishai kills.

items.quote: the city was calm, because Athaliah had been slain with the sword at the palace.
items.contrast: Athaliah’s death is given as the cause of the city’s calm; the people’s rejoicing is a separate concurrent outcome.
items.reason: The explicit causal marker “because” links the city’s calm to Athaliah having been slain at the palace.
